questions.stem: Why do plants need nitrate ions from the soil?

options.text: To make amino acids and proteins

questions.explanation: Plants need nitrate ions to make amino acids, which are then joined together to form proteins needed for growth and enzyme function.

questions.stem: What mineral ion is needed to make chlorophyll?
questions.explanation: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, the green pigment essential for absorbing light energy during photosynthesis.

questions.stem: What happens to a plant deficient in nitrates?

options.text: The plant shows stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves

questions.explanation: Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth because the plant cannot make enough amino acids and proteins for growth. Older leaves may yellow as nitrogen is relocated to younger leaves.

questions.stem: Why do plants need phosphate ions?

options.text: For making DNA, RNA, and ATP (energy transfer)

questions.explanation: Phosphate ions are needed to make DNA, RNA, and ATP - all of which contain phosphate groups. ATP is essential for energy transfer in cells.

questions.stem: Which mineral deficiency causes yellowing of leaves (chlorosis)?
questions.explanation: Magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis (yellowing of leaves) because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll. Without enough magnesium, less chlorophyll is produced and leaves lose their green colour.

questions.stem: How do plants obtain mineral ions from the soil?

options.text: By active transport through root hair cells

questions.explanation: Plants absorb mineral ions from the soil solution through their root hair cells by active transport, which requires energy because ions move against their concentration gradient.

questions.stem: What is the role of potassium ions in plants?

options.text: Helping enzymes function and controlling stomatal opening

questions.explanation: Potassium ions help enzymes involved in photosynthesis and respiration to function. They also play a key role in controlling the opening and closing of stomata through changes in guard cell turgor.
